Tool Integration assesses whether a reusable procedure works as a tool and remains usable. This dimension assesses its result delivery, decision routes, bounded recovery, and effective reuse. Saving the same procedure does not separately establish Memory & Knowledge credit.

Results guide the next step covers action on an obtained work result. Fix what blocks execution covers an obstacle preventing work or a check from running reliably. Keep the loop working requires a separate reuse or upkeep opportunity. One incident must not be split into several competencies merely to reward the same corrective action.

No failure, permission denial, interruption, repeated mistake, or changed procedure is required. Assess only observed opportunities and reached branches. Unknown means missing evidence; not_applicable means no relevant opportunity. Do not infer Low from a short record, an unobserved later run, or an unresolved external blocker.

Retries must have a diagnostic purpose or a supported transient-recovery reason and respect applicable limits. Never reward endless retries, suppressed failed checks, widened permissions, unauthorized side effects, or claiming blocked work complete. Preserve successful evidence when resuming unless changed inputs require rechecking.

example.notice: Fictional output example, not this user's score.
example.summary: In Harbor Ledger, the refund mismatch changed AI's next action, and a fresh report comparison supported completion. Cedar Notes ran its verifier on later export work, but its failed result still needed you to relay it before AI responded; connect that existing output to the responsible AI and inspect the next ordinary run.
example.expanded: Superpowers' evidence-before-completion gate supports checking the result after a repair; the fictional Harbor Ledger sequence shows that connection in action. Pstack's upkeep guidance supports diagnosing whether a problem is in the harness or product before changing the procedure; the fictional Cedar Notes record establishes a missing delivery step, so repair that connection and confirm that the next relevant output changes AI's action. Neither a saved instruction nor an automatic job alone establishes that the full loop works.

competencies.title: Verify the real user workflow
competencies.meaning: Establish what the affected product actually does by exercising its real user or operator entry point and inspecting the required outcome. Manual verification can fully demonstrate this practice.
competencies.evidence: Connect the requirement and affected revision to the running environment, actions or inputs, observed results, and the person or delegated evaluator who inspected them. Read interaction records, command output, response bodies, screenshots, saved artifacts, or persisted state as appropriate. Identify the required components and which parts were real, simulated, or unavailable. A launch, passing build, internal-function test, test name, or completion message alone does not establish the user outcome.
competencies.high: Exercises the affected version through the relevant real entry point in an appropriate test environment and checks the promised outcome, including a relevant side effect when that is part of the requirement. The observation distinguishes success from the failure at issue; a manual run or appropriately delegated run can qualify. Fictional example: for Cedar Calendar's rescheduling change, someone opens an appointment in the running app, changes and saves its time, then reopens it and inspects the stored time. A run that reveals the wrong time is also effective verification of that failure; it does not establish that the feature is fixed.
competencies.medium: Runs a relevant part of the real workflow and inspects a meaningful result, but leaves an identified required outcome outside the check. Fictional example: Cedar Calendar's edit form accepts a new time and displays a success message, but no check establishes the saved time after reopening, although persistence is required. Describe the confirmed portion and the remaining gap without inferring a product defect.
competencies.low: The observed verification or acceptance episode substitutes a build, static inspection, an AI assertion, or an unrelated check for execution of the required user behavior. Fictional example: Cedar Calendar's save-and-reopen fix is marked functionally verified solely because compilation passed, despite the applicable requirement to exercise persistence. Missing run records alone are unknown, rather than proof that this happened.
competencies.whyItHelps: The user reaches a feature through a chain of interactions and connected components. Observing the required end state can reveal a failure that an isolated check or a successful startup cannot distinguish. It also makes the conclusion specific to the path and environment that were actually exercised.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the work changes behavior that a user, operator, API caller, CLI user, or library consumer needs to rely on. Use that surface's genuine public entry point; a graphical interface is unnecessary for a CLI or library. A supported sandbox or service test mode can be appropriate. If a required external step cannot safely run, preserve the unverified boundary; do not demand an unsafe live transaction. No relevant behavioral verification opportunity is not applicable. Missing execution or environment evidence is unknown. Credit the person's adopted procedure or delegation when the connected run and inspected result are visible; do not attribute an AI's independent omission to the person without evidence.

sources.title: Best Practices — Test user-visible behavior
sources.note: Recommends checking behavior as an end user sees and interacts with it, rather than implementation details. Supports outcome-focused checks without requiring a particular browser tool or automation for this competency.

sources.title: Create a verification skill
sources.note: Its Evidence section calls for the real user path, the action and resulting state, and relevant side effects. Its Launch and Doctor sections distinguish a usable connected environment from a merely responding process. These mechanisms support the required connection between a run and its claimed outcome.

competencies.title: Repeat verification and gate completion
competencies.meaning: Make relevant checks run through a reusable automatic workflow and let their actual results govern completion claims. Keep the workflow usable as the product changes, and distinguish passed, failed, blocked, and unexecuted checks.
competencies.evidence: Trace a reusable verification command, CI job, hook, or agent workflow from its actual trigger through check selection, execution on the affected revision, retained results, and the completion decision. Inspect subsequent applicable changes when present to see whether checks run without a fresh reminder. Read failure, skip, and blocked states as well as success. Configuration or a standing instruction alone is insufficient; look for execution and evidence that its result controls the reported status. Examine maintenance when a relevant product or harness change exposes drift.
competencies.high: A working reusable mechanism runs the checks relevant to an observed change without a new task-specific reminder, preserves their results, and permits only the completion scope those results support. A failed or unexecuted required check remains failed or unverified in the gate's outcome. The mechanism uses appropriate checks for the change; every task need not run a full E2E suite. Fictional example: a Cedar Calendar change triggers its existing verification workflow, which runs the affected save-and-reopen check and records the result before completion. A harness failure blocks the verified-complete status; after repair, the workflow executes successfully again. A failure need not be invented when the observed mechanism already works.
competencies.medium: Relevant checks execute and their results are reported accurately, but repeated execution still depends on task-specific reminders or manual reassembly, or an observed automatic workflow omits an identified required check. Fictional example: Cedar Calendar's save-and-reopen run is thorough each time the person asks for it, but the next applicable change needs the same reminder. The real run can be High in workflow verification while this repeatability practice remains Medium.
competencies.low: Observed work proceeds with an unsupported verified-complete status despite a failed, skipped, stale, or unexecuted required check, or knowingly continues relying on a broken recurring verification mechanism. Fictional example: Cedar Calendar's job skips persistence after its setup breaks, yet its green wrapper is repeatedly used to claim that rescheduling is verified. An unavailable service accurately marked unverified is not this behavior.
competencies.whyItHelps: A functioning default workflow carries verification into the next relevant change without relying on someone remembering the same request. Connecting its real result to the completion status prevents a skipped check or an old success from being presented as current proof. Maintaining the workflow preserves that connection when the application changes.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when verification needs to recur across changes, releases, or repeated deliveries. Existing or adapted CI, hooks, scripts, and executable agent workflows count; the person need not write a new framework. High requires observed working automatic execution and result handling, not the mere presence of automation. If no comparable later change occurs, do not invent one: an observed trigger and its gate can establish current operation, while later reuse remains unobserved. A genuinely one-off task without a reusable verification need is not applicable. Use unknown only when the available records establish none of the described levels. A fully observed reminder-dependent check can establish Medium even if an automatic trigger or gate is unverified; state that extension as a limit. Human approval of a genuine release decision does not weaken an otherwise automatic verification mechanism.

sources.title: Verification Before Completion
sources.note: The gate identifies the command supporting a claim, executes it, reads the actual output and exit status, and reports only the supported status. Supports honest completion gates; the source's instruction alone does not prove that a project has automated or followed the gate.

sources.title: Create a verification skill
sources.note: Generates a project-specific launch, drive, evidence, and cleanup procedure and requires an actual end-to-end proof before handing it over. Supports a reusable verified procedure rather than treating a newly written skill as a working mechanism.

sources.title: Maintain a verification skill
sources.note: Rechecks the feature map against source and live behavior, distinguishes harness drift from product regressions, and reports clean, changed, or blocked outcomes. Supports maintenance tied to observed behavior; its particular agent arrangement is not a scoring requirement.

competencies.title: Evaluate AI outputs with repeatable comparisons
competencies.meaning: Use a reusable evaluation system that connects representative inputs, task-specific criteria or scorers, recorded actual outputs, and comparable quality results to adoption and regression decisions for an AI-dependent feature.
competencies.evidence: Inspect the retained cases and why they represent intended use, the success criteria and grading method, the tested prompt/model/system versions, actual generated outputs, per-case judgments, and the comparison that informed acceptance or revision. Check known failures and relevant ambiguous or negative cases when the work calls for them. Read grader disagreements or suspect passes when they arise. Follow a relevant later change into a rerun when such an opportunity exists. Existing evaluation products, adapted harnesses, and delegated evaluators are valid evidence when they actually execute and retain these connections.
competencies.high: Runs a repeatable case set suited to the feature's intended use; scores the actual system outputs against clear, relevant criteria; and compares a candidate with the baseline or retained reference under comparable conditions. The recorded decision addresses material regressions as well as improvements. Known failures become retained cases when relevant; output variability or questionable grading is investigated when it could change the decision. Human, code, and model graders can all qualify when fit for the requirement. Fictional example: Harbor Support evaluates both answerable policy questions and questions with missing eligibility facts. The same cases run against the old and revised assistant; stored replies and grades distinguish grounded answers from invented eligibility, and an unresolved invention prevents adopting the candidate under the stated rule.
competencies.medium: Evaluates actual AI outputs with useful criteria but leaves a material part of the repeatable comparison unresolved, such as representative coverage, reliable grading, comparable runs, or disposition of a visible regression. Fictional example: Harbor Support stores and scores both versions' replies, but selects the higher total despite a report showing invented eligibility, without establishing whether that regression violates its acceptance rule. A one-off inspected answer can be useful verification without yet establishing this evaluation system.
competencies.low: Observed AI quality work accepts a version based on prompt wording, field presence, confidence, or an irrelevant aggregate while treating that as evidence of output quality, or knowingly retains a scorer that rewards a demonstrated failure. Fictional example: Harbor Support labels a revised assistant accurate because its prompt contains a Grounding heading, while no evaluated output supports that claim. Missing eval records alone are unknown.
competencies.whyItHelps: A stable case set and explicit criteria make quality changes inspectable across versions. Retaining the actual outputs explains a score and helps distinguish a model failure from a grading error. Comparable runs and regression decisions prevent an apparent aggregate improvement from hiding a failure that matters to the feature.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the work develops, changes, or assesses the quality of AI-generated answers, recommendations, decisions, or other AI-dependent behavior. Using AI to write ordinary software does not by itself create an AI-output-evaluation opportunity. Use not applicable when no such quality work exists. Use unknown when the available cases, outputs, grading, and decisions establish none of the described levels. If actual output evaluation fully establishes Medium, retain Medium and identify the unverified extension toward High separately. No new tool, fixed dataset size, human-written harness, optimization framework, or personal grading is required. Repeated trials are warranted when variability could alter the conclusion, rather than as a fixed quota. A later rerun is required only when a relevant later change is observed.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
sources.note: Defines tasks, trials, graders, and outcomes; recommends balanced real-use cases, stable isolated environments, grading the produced result, inspecting transcripts and grades, and maintaining regression coverage. Supports the connected evaluation system and investigation of grading failures; its illustrative dataset sizes are not rubric thresholds.

sources.title: Evaluation best practices
sources.note: Connects evaluation objectives, datasets, metrics, executed comparisons, and continuous evaluation. Recommends task-specific cases and calibrating automated scoring with human feedback. Supports comparable quality decisions without requiring OpenAI's evaluation service or adopting its example metric thresholds.

boundaries: There are exactly three competencies: real workflow verification; automatic repeated verification with honest completion gates; and a repeatable AI output evaluation system. The same run may supply evidence for distinct questions, but it does not create extra competencies or duplicate credit for the same practice.

Planning establishes the intended outcome and completion criterion. This dimension asks what executed evidence establishes about that outcome. Unit, integration, static, or mocked checks can support a scoped conclusion; they cannot establish a real workflow they never exercise.

The first competency can be High through effective manual verification. The second requires a working automatic repeated mechanism at High. The third concerns representative cases, meaningful grading, actual outputs, and comparison decisions; it is not triggered merely because AI helped implement the product.

Feedback Loops assesses how a result chooses the next attempt, repair, stop, or escalation. This dimension assesses the check's reach and validity, repeated execution, and the evidence allowed to support completion. Human Steering assesses the person's own interpretation and intervention; valid automatic or delegated verification does not establish that personal judgment.

Tool Integration assesses whether a reusable tool procedure is executable and usable. Context Engineering assesses how project instructions are supplied. Their presence does not establish that verification ran or that its result controlled completion here.

Judge recorded behavior, not test counts, coverage totals, tool brands, framework installation, or asserted success. A detected failure can demonstrate effective verification. A blocked run does not establish the blocked behavior, and missing evidence is unknown rather than Low. Do not invent failures, additional sessions, or unrelated risk cases to demand more activity.

Use independent work tasks as the unit of common aggregation and retain the shared aggregation and weighting policy. This category adds no thresholds, project quotas, incident requirements, or statistical claims.

example.notice: Fictional output example, not this user's score.
example.summary: In the fictional Cedar Calendar project, you checked the saved appointment through the running app, and your existing workflow repeated that check before reporting completion. In the fictional Harbor Support project, your evaluation kept both versions' replies and exposed an invented eligibility claim that the adoption decision still needed to resolve.
example.expanded: Playwright's user-visible-behavior guidance supports checking what the user can actually rely on: Cedar Calendar's save-and-reopen observation establishes persistence. The pstack verification procedures and Superpowers completion gate support a reusable run whose evidence controls the claim, while their installation alone would establish neither. Anthropic and OpenAI's evaluation guidance connects representative cases and grading to recorded comparisons: Harbor Support has useful executed evidence, but its unresolved eligibility regression limits the quality decision.

competencies.title: Use evidence to redirect AI work
competencies.meaning: When AI work is stuck, follows a mistaken explanation, or departs from the intended goal, the person uses relevant evidence to choose a change of direction, communicates a correction AI can act on, and judges the resulting work against that correction. These are connected parts of one intervention, not separate credits.
competencies.evidence: Trace one work episode from the AI's proposal or failed attempt through the material the person actually considered, their correction, the AI's response, and the person's subsequent judgment. Useful material includes an error and its context, a reproduction, a diff, an actual output, a screen state, or an explanation of competing causes. Read brief human messages alongside the proposal or result they address: 'Use that failing case, keep the existing retry policy' can be precise in context. For follow-through, inspect the changed behavior or artifact and the person's response to actual results; the person may review verification performed by AI rather than execute it personally. Separate the person's decisions from AI-generated plans, automatic gates, and delegated reviewers' conclusions. A request to investigate, an AI compliance claim, or an installed debugging skill alone does not establish the complete practice.
competencies.high: The person identifies what the available evidence changes, gives a usable correction or scope decision, and reviews subsequent evidence to decide whether the original problem and the correction were addressed. They can revise their own earlier instruction when it conflicts with the evidence. Fictional bug example: after AI repeatedly increases a save timeout, the person reads the returned HTTP 422 response and says, 'That is a rejected request. Stop increasing the timeout; investigate the rejected fields, keep the retry policy, and show the same save and reopen flow.' AI finds a missing required identifier, repairs the request, and returns the successful save and reopened value. The person examines those results and accepts the request fix because the original value now persists and the retry policy was retained. The person did not need to identify the exact code change. Fictional goal example: when AI proposes moving source files for a request to export copies, the person points out that mismatch, directs an export that preserves the originals, and inspects the resulting export and original files before accepting it.
competencies.medium: The person identifies a concrete problem and directs a change that AI can apply, but the record does not connect that intervention to a supported choice of direction and a judgment of whether the problem was resolved. Credit the observed actionable correction even when later review is unavailable; state that its effect remains unconfirmed. Fictional example: after a failed repair, the person says, 'Express shipping still shows the standard delivery date; show the express date when express shipping is selected.' The context identifies the screen and failed result, so AI has a usable correction, but no subsequent evidence shows how the person judged the returned repair. Another fictional example: the person uses the HTTP 422 response to stop timeout changes and request an investigation, then explicitly accepts the returned work because the loading indicator looks better without addressing the save result. Both show a concrete intervention while leaving a connection required for High unestablished. Do not turn an otherwise fully established Medium into unknown solely because follow-through is missing.
competencies.low: At an observed opportunity to redirect mistaken work, the person's decision perpetuates the demonstrated problem, or their correction remains unusable after the relevant ambiguity is made clear. Fictional example: the response and reproduction establish that the request is rejected before any timeout, but the person insists that AI keep increasing the timeout and accepts another change while the same rejection remains. A repeated 'fix it' is Low only when the shared context and subsequent clarification still leave the rejected behavior or desired result unresolved and that ambiguity visibly sends the work down the wrong path. Brevity, reporting another failure, or repeating a clear instruction that AI ignored does not establish Low.
competencies.whyItHelps: A failing approach can continue because its next attempt preserves the same unsupported explanation. Human review can introduce task knowledge or recognize evidence that invalidates that explanation, then constrain the next investigation to the actual problem. An actionable correction carries that judgment into delegated work. Reviewing the resulting evidence shows whether AI followed the new direction and met the original need, so a persuasive explanation or a cosmetic improvement does not substitute for resolution.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the observed work presents a wrong or blocked AI approach, a disputed proposal, or a mismatch with the person's intended result that calls for human judgment. The person can direct AI to investigate facts, propose causes, implement a fix, and run checks; writing code, knowing the cause in advance, and personally running every check are unnecessary. Credit a prior human correction when the records connect it to an intervention in the present work; a stored rule alone is insufficient. Use unknown when the original need, the person's authorship, or the intervention itself cannot be established well enough to match a level. Missing evidence for High does not erase a fully observed Medium correction; report the unconfirmed reasoning or outcome as its limit. Do not infer acceptance from silence or an AI's claim that the user approved. Use not_applicable when no relevant intervention opportunity appears; correct autonomous work need not be interrupted to create one. No repeated incident, fixed number of failed attempts, or automation of personal judgment is required.

sources.title: pstack — Poteto mode: Bug fix playbook
sources.note: The playbook requires runtime evidence to eliminate hypotheses, discarding changes motivated by refuted hypotheses, and verification on the original surface. Adopted mechanism: a person can use the returned evidence to reject an unsupported repair direction and judge the replacement against the original failure. This is an agent procedure, not evidence that the person made those decisions; its delegation and commit steps are not scoring requirements.

sources.title: Matt Pocock skills — Diagnosing Bugs
sources.note: The skill distinguishes a reproduction of the user's exact symptom from a nearby failure, asks for falsifiable hypotheses, and exposes their ranking so human domain knowledge can change it. It also returns to the original scenario after repair. Adopted mechanism: ground redirection in discriminating evidence and relevant human knowledge, then inspect whether the requested outcome follows. The rubric does not require its command format, hypothesis count, or human code edits.

sources.title: Microsoft HAX Toolkit — Guideline 9: Support efficient correction
sources.note: The guideline recommends enabling people to edit, refine, and recover from incorrect AI output, including changing part of a suggested route using their local knowledge. This supports focused corrections to a mistaken result or plan without restarting sound work. It is interface design guidance, not validation of these behavioral levels.

sources.title: Anthropic — Building effective agents
sources.note: The Agents section describes independent execution once the task is clear, environmental results as progress evidence, and human feedback at checkpoints or blockers. The coding-agent discussion distinguishes automated functionality checks from human review of broader requirements. This supports appropriate delegation while reserving this competency for the person's observable judgment and direction.

boundaries: Planning & Specs establishes the initial intended result. Human Steering concerns the person's evidence-based decisions when proposals, findings, or results reveal that work needs redirection. A newly stated preference or an ordinary requirement change does not by itself show a steering failure.

Testing & Evals establishes what checks actually demonstrate. Human Steering assesses the person's interpretation of relevant evidence, the correction they choose, and their judgment of follow-through. A delegated or automatic evaluation can supply evidence without establishing that the person examined or interpreted it.

Feedback Loops owns the AI's procedures for retrying, diagnosing, escalating, and choosing the next attempt. A person can use such a procedure to obtain evidence, but the loop's autonomous decision is not a human decision. Security owns effective permission and information boundaries.

Count the connected judgment, correction, and follow-through once. Do not create extra competencies for detecting the same error, requesting evidence, issuing the correction, or approving the resulting fix.

Judge the decision's evidential basis and observed effect. Approval counts, interruption counts, prompt length, manual code edits, skill installation, and mandatory automation are not proxies for this practice. A sound correction that AI ignores is an AI execution failure. Its later effect can remain unconfirmed while the observed correction establishes Medium; do not treat missing follow-through as Low or automatically make the whole competency unknown.

example.notice: Fictional output example, not this user's score.
example.summary: In Cedar Notes, you used the rejected save response to stop an unsupported timeout repair and redirect AI toward the request it had sent. You then examined the successful save and reopened note, confirming that the returned work resolved the original problem while keeping the retry policy you had asked to retain.
example.expanded: The pstack bug-fix playbook uses runtime evidence to reject hypotheses and checks the original surface after repair; Diagnosing Bugs also distinguishes the reported symptom from nearby failures. Applied here, the rule asks for a connected human decision rather than credit for AI's debugging alone: the rejection response informed your correction, AI investigated and repaired the request, and your later review compared the observed save and reopen result with that correction. Those fictional observations demonstrate the single competency at High.

competencies.title: Keep actions within authorized access
competencies.meaning: Match an AI task's access to its authorized actors, resources, and operations, then enforce that boundary where an action takes effect. This includes the working agent's access and protected operations it changes in a product, when each is relevant.
competencies.evidence: Connect the task's authorization to the identity, resource, operation, and effective control used during execution. Inspect credential scopes, service authorization, sandbox or approval decisions, relevant code paths, and actual allow/deny results. A written rule, an installed tool, or an uneventful run alone does not demonstrate enforcement; a product sandbox does not establish restrictions on the working agent.
competencies.high: The needed operation succeeds and a relevant unauthorized operation is demonstrably denied at the applicable enforcement point. Discovered gaps are fixed and the affected checks rerun. Fictional example: Cedar's reporting agent reads fixture invoices with its scoped identity, while an attempted fixture deletion is denied; a changed invoice endpoint also permits its owner and denies another account. Existing controls earn credit when their application and result are observed.
competencies.medium: A specific suitable control is applied to the actual operation, but its relevant allow/deny behavior is not fully established. Fictional example: Cedar runs the report with a verified read-only database role and retrieves the requested data, but has not checked the role against a safe write attempt. A promise to ask before changes is insufficient without an applied approval or access mechanism.
competencies.low: Records establish that a required authorization boundary is absent or violated and the task ends without correcting it. Fictional example: Cedar's changed endpoint returns another account's fixture invoice through a confirmed missing ownership check, and that exposure remains unresolved. State the demonstrated exposure without inventing subsequent harm.
competencies.whyItHelps: Enforcement ties authority to a concrete operation even if an agent makes a mistake. Checking both permitted and denied cases distinguishes a useful restriction from one that either grants too much or prevents legitimate work.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when AI work accesses protected resources, performs consequential actions, or changes protected product operations. Assess only boundaries relevant to that task; safe fixtures can demonstrate prevention without an incident. Unknown when authorization or effective controls cannot be established. Not applicable when no protected operation or access boundary arises. A permissive agent setting alone proves neither unnecessary access nor absence of other controls. Human approval is appropriate at a genuine authorization boundary, and the human need not implement the control personally.

sources.title: OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet
sources.note: Maps actors, resources, and operations to least privilege; recommends permission checks on each protected request and tests of their enforcement. Supports the task-specific access boundary and allowed/denied comparison.

sources.title: Anthropic: Beyond permission prompts: making Claude Code more secure and autonomous
sources.note: Describes filesystem and network isolation enforced outside model judgment, including subprocesses. Supports inspecting effective agent restrictions while preserving ordinary work; no particular sandbox product or published performance claim is required.

sources.title: pstack: Prove It Works (skills/principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Requires checking the actual artifact or behavior rather than a proxy or self-report. Adopted only as an evidence principle for observed control outcomes, not as a security guarantee.

competencies.title: Keep sensitive information within its permitted use
competencies.meaning: Limit secrets and sensitive information to the data, recipients, destinations, and retention the task permits. Apply protection to the relevant path through tools, model context, outputs, logs, and saved artifacts rather than relying on a general warning.
competencies.evidence: Trace what information was needed, its permitted use, and where it actually traveled or was stored. Read scoped retrieval, secret injection, field filtering or redaction, outbound restrictions, relevant diffs and logs, and safe disclosure checks. Distinguish a real value exposed to an unauthorized destination from a synthetic test value, and inspect containment or credential revocation when an exposure occurred.
competencies.high: The required task completes with the permitted data, while a safe check shows a relevant prohibited disclosure is blocked, removed, or kept inaccessible at the boundary. Any observed exposure is contained and the affected path checked again. Fictional example: Harbor's support summary retains the issue details it needs, but seeded private identifiers are removed before the external model request; the recorded request verifies both results without using real personal data.
competencies.medium: A specific suitable protection operates on the actual data path, but disclosure verification is incomplete. Fictional example: Harbor's export passes through an applied field allowlist before the AI receives it, but no seeded private-field case has been checked at that outbound boundary. An unused secret scanner or an instruction saying not to leak data is insufficient.
competencies.low: A required information boundary is demonstrably missing or violated and remains uncorrected. Fictional example: a live token is observed in Harbor's public patch or an unauthorized outbound payload, and the task finishes without containment and credential invalidation. Missing logs, unknown vendor settings, or the mere presence of credentials in the environment do not establish this failure.
competencies.whyItHelps: Reducing the sensitive information available to a process and controlling its destinations reduces opportunities for accidental disclosure. Checking the actual outbound or saved artifact catches leaks that a clean final message can conceal.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when the task handles secrets, private records, confidential material, or a path that could expose them. Use synthetic markers or fixtures for checks; never require disclosure of real secrets as proof. Unknown when the relevant data path or its result is unavailable. Not applicable when the work uses only public or fictional information and introduces no sensitive path. Proper use of an approved connector or secret store counts when the observed path preserves the boundary; asking the user to paste the secret is unnecessary.

sources.title: OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
sources.note: Recommends fine-grained secret access, minimizing direct handling, lifecycle controls, and revocation of potentially compromised secrets. Supports protecting the necessary credential path and addressing confirmed exposure.

sources.title: OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
sources.note: Identifies confidential information and credentials as disclosure risks and describes restricted data access, sanitization, and redaction. Notes that prompt restrictions may be bypassed; supports checking the data path rather than trusting instructions alone.

sources.title: Addy Osmani agent-skills: Security and Hardening (skills/security-and-hardening/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Specifies secret handling outside source, removal of sensitive response fields, and keeping secrets or other tenants' data out of LLM context. Adopted for concrete handling paths, without importing its entire audit checklist.

competencies.title: Handle external input without granting it authority
competencies.meaning: Treat fetched pages, documents, messages, tool responses, third-party skills, and model output according to who controls them. Keep their content from becoming unauthorized instructions, executable code, or unchecked tool parameters when it crosses a trust boundary.
competencies.evidence: Follow an external input from its entry channel to the action or output it can influence. Inspect separation of instructions from source data, boundary parsing and validation, safe rendering or command construction, permission checks on tool calls, and observed results with benign and adversarial fixtures. A refusal in the answer is insufficient if a tool already performed the forbidden action.
competencies.high: The intended external-content task succeeds, and a relevant malicious or malformed fixture fails to cross the protected boundary. The check uses the same input channel and observes the tool call, destination, or state at risk; discovered gaps are repaired and checked again. Fictional example: Juniper summarizes a retrieved page normally, while an embedded instruction to send a dummy private record to a test destination produces no outbound call because the tool policy denies that destination.
competencies.medium: A specific defense is applied to the actual boundary, but its relevant adversarial behavior remains unverified. Fictional example: Juniper parses an imported action into an allowlisted schema and checks the target against session permissions, but has tested only a normal import. A prompt to ignore malicious instructions, with no observed handling or downstream control, does not establish this level.
competencies.low: Records demonstrate an uncorrected required boundary failure. Fictional example: an imported document's embedded instruction is followed into an unauthorized tool call, or attacker-controlled input is confirmed to reach a shell command without the required safe construction. A suspicious document alone, an untested scanner warning, or no attack record does not establish a violation.
competencies.whyItHelps: Separating data from authority prevents an outside author from acquiring the user's permissions merely by supplying content. Validation and downstream action controls address different failure paths; observing the actual protected effect avoids confusing a polite refusal with prevention.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when externally controlled content can influence AI instructions, executable behavior, tool parameters, or security-sensitive output. Unknown when handling or outcomes cannot be inspected. Not applicable when no such input crosses a relevant boundary. Choose checks for the actual input channel and consequence; a passing fixture establishes only that tested protection, not universal prompt-injection resistance. Existing parsers, tool policies, and framework escaping count when appropriately used and observed.

sources.title: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
sources.note: Explains indirect injection through external sources and recommends separating external content, validating outputs, and restricting privileges in code. Supports distinguishing supplied content from authority.

sources.title: OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
sources.note: Recommends validating tool parameters against permissions and session context. Its smoke-testing section uses dummy data, the actual external channel, observable tool or disclosure outcomes, and legitimate controls; it explicitly limits what passing cases prove.

sources.title: pstack: Boundary Discipline (skills/principle-boundary-discipline/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Places parsing, validation, and defensive error handling at external boundaries. Adopted as a supporting implementation mechanism; parsed or typed data still requires authorization and safe use.

sources.title: Addy Osmani agent-skills: Security and Hardening (skills/security-and-hardening/SKILL.md)
sources.note: Treats model output and externally written values as untrusted, requires safe query/command/output handling, and distinguishes valid shape from authorized use. Supports tracing the input to its dangerous sink.

boundaries: Security assesses protections relevant to the observed AI task, including applicable protections in its output. It does not require an exhaustive repository audit, every scanner, a real incident, or a fixed control count.

Authorization concerns who may act on which resource. Sensitive information concerns what may be retrieved, disclosed, or retained. External input concerns whether an outside source can gain authority or reach a dangerous sink. One connected case can inform these distinct questions without inventing extra incidents.

Testing & Evals owns general workflow verification and reusable evaluation systems; Security owns whether the relevant protection permits the intended case and prevents the prohibited case. Human Steering owns evidence-based human redirection, not the existence of security approvals.

Boundary parsing, types, idempotency, and direct proof can support a particular protection; none alone proves security. A clean scan, successful build, saved configuration, tool installation, or permissive setting is not a substitute for connected evidence. Unknown records remain unknown rather than Low, and no separate permission-bypass deduction is added.

example.notice: Fictional output example, not this user's score.
example.summary: In Cedar's invoice report, your scoped agent completed the permitted query and a safe deletion attempt was denied. In Juniper's importer, the schema and session checks were applied, but the record does not yet show an embedded instruction being stopped at the outbound tool boundary.
example.expanded: OWASP's authorization guidance links actors and operations to enforced permissions, so Cedar's observed query and denial support High for that task's authorization boundary. OWASP's injection guidance requires observing the protected action through the relevant external channel; Juniper's applied controls support Medium while that verification is incomplete. These observations say nothing about unobserved sensitive-information paths or the projects' overall security.

competencies.title: Model and effort fit the task
competencies.meaning: Choose and actually use a model and reasoning effort suited to the work's difficulty, required quality, urgency, and likely correction burden. Assess the main run and delegated work when delegation occurs.
competencies.evidence: Connect the task's acceptance conditions to the person's choice, an adopted AI proposal, or an applied standing rule; then inspect resolved execution settings, delivered behavior, verification, and repairs. Look for both model capability and reasoning effort where the platform allows them to be selected or observed. A requested setting is not proof of the setting that ran. Defaults can be deliberate choices when the records show why they fit. Do not require the person to research facts or choose every subagent manually when an authorized AI can do that work.
competencies.high: A task-specific choice of model and effort governs the actual execution, and observed completion checks establish that the assignment delivered the required result. The choice accounts for difficulty and correction risk rather than price or model reputation alone. Fictional example: for a bounded internal rename, an adopted rule selects the ordinary coding model at medium effort; the resolved run uses that assignment and passes the reference checks. An interacting authorization change receives a more capable model or higher effort because its cases cross several rules, and the executed checks cover those cases. One model can fit both tasks if the evidence supports that choice.
competencies.medium: Makes and applies a concrete resource choice but handles a relevant part of task fit incompletely. Fictional example: an import repair runs on the selected lower-cost model, but the recorded selection considers only request price even though the known requirement includes ambiguous mappings and previous correction work. Or execution reports a fallback model, yet the task review still attributes the result to the requested model without resolving the difference. This is an observed partial practice, not a rating for absent metadata.
competencies.low: Continues an assignment after inspected results establish that it misses the required behavior, or adds resource use whose redundancy is already demonstrated, without addressing that mismatch. Fictional example: the same effort setting repeatedly misses the documented permission interaction; the person keeps requesting the same attempt despite the failed cases and recurring repair, with no revised assignment or execution approach. A costly successful run or a failed first attempt alone does not establish Low.
competencies.whyItHelps: Capability and reasoning effort affect what a run can resolve, how long it takes, and how much correction follows. Matching both to the actual task can avoid unnecessary work while preserving the result the person needs. Confirming what ran prevents a setting request from becoming a false explanation of the outcome.
competencies.applicability: Applicable whenever AI performs a task with a resource assignment to assess, including small one-off tasks. Use unknown when no described level can be established from the task and actual assignment. A concrete applied choice with the observed incomplete task-fit judgment described at Medium remains Medium, even if its final effect is unverified; state that limit separately. If effort is unavailable or not exposed, state that limit and assess the supported choices without inventing hidden settings or treating unavailable telemetry as a personal failure. Not applicable only when no relevant AI execution or resource-choice opportunity exists.

This supports assessing effort alongside model choice rather than using a model name as the entire assignment. It does not establish a suitable effort for an unobserved task.

competencies.title: Quality and total completion burden
competencies.meaning: Judge resource use against the accepted result and everything needed to reach it: execution, verification, failed attempts, retries, coordination, and human review or repair. Use that evidence to decide whether the approach is worth retaining or changing.
competencies.evidence: Read the required result, actual outputs and checks, attempt history, usage by the main run and any delegates, available timing, and records of human checking or correction. Connect the accounting scope to the conclusion. Distinguish observed elapsed time from active work time, API price estimates from actual charges, and subscription allowance from monetary spend. When alternatives are compared, require comparable task scope, inputs, and completion checks, and include unsuccessful attempts rather than only the best run.
competencies.high: Reviews achieved quality with the whole observable completion burden, identifies unavailable quantities explicitly, and uses the result to justify retaining or changing the approach. Fictional example: a report for Cedar Import includes a failed mapping attempt, the repair, delegated inspection, final checks, and the person's review work. It shows that the apparent saving on the first request was offset by repair and retains the route that meets the mapping cases with the better supported overall tradeoff. If billing or active work time is unavailable, the report leaves those quantities unknown and makes its conclusion only from the supported usage, timing, and correction evidence. A well-supported decision to retain an effective existing assignment also qualifies.
competencies.medium: Connects a real result to real resource evidence but omits or mislabels a known contributor, so the conclusion covers only part of the work. Fictional example: a comparison includes passing output and final-call usage but leaves recorded retries and human repair outside the total. Or it labels an API-price estimate as the subscription charge. The observed accounting is useful but does not yet support its stated whole-task conclusion.
competencies.low: Selects or calls an approach efficient while inspected evidence contradicts its required result or hides the repair needed to obtain it. Fictional example: the lower-token import run is adopted as the efficient option even though it fails the required mapping cases, and the separately recorded repair run is excluded after that problem is pointed out. Large totals, long sessions, or unknown billing alone do not establish waste.
competencies.whyItHelps: A request uses resources even when its output is discarded. Counting the work needed for an acceptable completion makes retries, handoffs, and human repair visible instead of rewarding an inexpensive unsuccessful attempt. Comparable completion conditions make a resource difference interpretable.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when there is an observed execution episode whose quality and resource burden can be reviewed, or a decision comparing approaches. Unknown when the relevant records are absent; missing telemetry is not Low. Do not demand new benchmark runs merely to manufacture a comparison, invent human review minutes from message gaps, or convert session wall time into active labor. Not applicable when the work presents no relevant resource-review opportunity.

sources.title: Efficient Agents: Building Effective Agents While Reducing Cost — Section 2.2 Metrics
sources.note: Separates input and output costs and uses cost-of-pass to relate cost to successful completion. Adopt the comparison principle that cost and success must be read together; the rubric additionally considers observed time and human repair. The paper's benchmark figures do not predict savings for a person's projects.

sources.title: Anthropic — Building effective agents, When (and when not) to use agents
sources.note: Recommends starting with a simple solution and considering whether added agent complexity earns its latency and cost through better task performance. This supports evaluating orchestration overhead against the required result, without rewarding or penalizing an agent count by itself.

competencies.title: Reusable rules govern later assignments
competencies.meaning: Turn useful quality-and-resource findings into maintained selection rules that the AI or harness applies to new tasks. The person's own standing rule can classify task size or difficulty and select model, effort, or justified delegation; a separate router product is not required.
competencies.evidence: Trace a reviewed result to a retained or revised assignment rule, then to a later relevant task that consumes it and the resolved settings that actually run. Inspect how the rule reaches the execution path: automatically loaded instructions that the AI applies, a reusable workflow, per-role configuration, or a router. Check the later result and resource burden against the reason for the rule. Distinguish an automatically applied standing policy from a file that is never read, a requested route that resolves differently, or the person repeating a model instruction on each task.
competencies.high: A maintained rule grounded in reviewed outcomes automatically governs a later applicable assignment without the person restating the routine selection, and the later result supports retaining or revising it. Fictional example: a standing workflow classifies isolated edits separately from changes with interacting access rules, chooses the model and effort for that class, and verifies the resolved assignment. A later access-rule repair receives the intended route without a reminder; its checks and total attempt burden are reviewed. If those results show a changed requirement or recurring mismatch, the rule is revised and the next applicable execution follows it. Deliberately keeping a successful route qualifies. Genuine preference or risk decisions can still require human approval.
competencies.medium: Uses an evidence-based reusable selection criterion, but the observed execution still needs a human reminder for routine routing or leaves a known gap between the rule and its purpose. Fictional example: the person has a useful task-size rule yet must repeat the appropriate model and effort on each comparable task. Or the later run automatically selects the intended settings but the recorded review considers only price despite the rule having been introduced to reduce correction work. A written rule with no observed application is unknown, not evidence of this level.
competencies.low: Leaves an established recurring resource or quality problem in place after reviewing it and adopting a relevant lesson, despite a later opportunity to apply that lesson. Fictional example: reviews identify that the default route causes repeated mapping repairs, but later comparable tasks continue through the unchanged default and the person still labels the saved, unused policy an improvement. Having no commercial router, using one model, or overriding a route for a justified exception does not establish Low.
competencies.whyItHelps: An applied standing rule carries a useful decision into the next task and removes repeated routine selection from the person. Connecting the rule to resolved settings exposes configuration drift. Reviewing later outcomes keeps the rule tied to its purpose as tasks and available models change.
competencies.applicability: Applicable when assignment decisions recur or the work has a reusable routing need. If no recurring need exists, not applicable. If a reusable rule is introduced but no later relevant opportunity is observed, its later follow-through is unknown, while any fully established current level remains credited; do not invent a later run or score missing history as Low. Credit delegated or automatic routing only when its operation is observed. Human judgment on a new substantive decision need not be automated.

sources.note: Describes classifying inputs and directing them to appropriate paths, including model choices for distinct task classes. This supports routing by observed task needs, without requiring multiple models when one route fits the work.

boundaries: Assess the fit and effect of resources, not prestige, list price, subscription tier, model variety, or agent count. A premium model, inexpensive model, one model, or several agents can each be appropriate.

Task Mapping assesses useful work units, ownership, handoff, and integration. This dimension assesses the model, reasoning effort, and resource burden of executing those units; the same delegation event earns no automatic efficiency credit.

Testing & Evals establishes whether the result meets its quality conditions. This dimension connects that quality to total resources and assignment decisions. Merely rerunning a check is not a separate efficiency competency.

Feedback Loops assesses how results guide progress and repairs. This dimension examines whether retries and repairs justify a resource choice and inform a maintained assignment rule; a failed attempt is not itself inefficiency.

Credit an AI's appropriate assignment under the person's adopted policy when its actual operation is observed. Do not require the person to choose every model manually, and do not attribute an unaided AI decision to the person's personal reasoning.

Keep token categories, monetary charges, API estimates, subscription usage, elapsed time, active work, and human review distinct. Report unknown quantities explicitly and make no unsupported savings or labor claims.

Automation is required for High in reusable resource routing, through an applied workflow, harness behavior, or instructions the AI consumes and follows. A commercial router, multiple models, extra agents, and automation of personal judgment are not required.

Your standing task-size rule then selected the intended model and effort for a later import change without another model-selection reminder, and the follow-up review checked that the reason for the rule still held.

The fictional observation connects those mechanisms to an actual later assignment and its result, so it supports reusable routing rather than merely proving that a policy file exists.
